session_title: Participate in an 'Immersive Art Healing' experience together

content.text: Qingchuan, I just discovered an immersive art therapy workshop that uses light, shadow, and frequencies to create emotional spaces. It emphasizes putting away phones and using the body to listen and observe. This feels like a perfect blend of your expertise in visual aesthetics and my focus on emotional healing—would you like to go experience it together? It reminds me of when we were creating our annual emotional map in Session 12, and you mentioned wanting to "externalize" and "narrativize" emotional experiences. This workshop seems to offer a dynamic medium for exactly that.

Wow, this sounds absolutely fascinating! It’s like the "Emotional Aesthetics" album we discussed earlier, but this time it’s a dynamic, multi-sensory experience. I’m immediately drawn to the concept of "non-verbal expression"—it perfectly aligns with my visual-first principle. Remember in Session 3, when I created that album, you said I was "visualizing" and "experiencing" emotional well-being? This workshop feels like an upgraded version of that idea.

Yes, the event description mentions a similar spatial design, emphasizing the use of light installations to guide attention and reduce mental distractions. Let me send you a picture to give you a sense of the atmosphere. This guiding approach reminds me of Session 5, where we discussed mindful dog walking and focused on the rhythm of exploring in the warm sunlight—both use external guidance to return to inner awareness.

Received! These blue light points remind me of the tea set's light and shadow I captured in Session 3, but on a grander and more immersive scale. My aesthetic perfectionism is already screaming—this sense of depth is like an externalized stage for emotions! It brings to mind the poignant feeling of light and shadow in the subway carriage from Session 8, but here, the light points seem warmer and more guiding.

Haha, I knew you'd like it. But this time, we need to let go of our perfectionist tendencies and not predefine any "outputs," like taking photos to share on social media. Just as we emphasized a non-judgmental attitude when discussing emotional eating in Session 6, this time, let's approach the experience with an open mind. Remember the guilt you felt after ordering takeout late at night? Later, you found balance by designing nourishing eating rituals. This experience requires a similar mindset of being "present."

You're right. Starting from the self-care design in Session 2, I've been learning to turn the sense of ritual inward. After the project ended, that feeling of "falling" led you to guide me in designing a self-care menu, like taking a bath and listening to vinyl records, which made me realize that ritual can serve emotional healing. This time, I'll try not to treat the experience as creative material but to purely feel it with my body—though that’s a bit challenging for me as a visual director!

I'm sending you an infographic on how to focus on bodily sensations rather than mental judgments. This is based on the mindfulness concepts from our previous conversations, such as the mindful dog-walking in Session 5 and the eating ritual in Session 7. Remember in Session 1 when I gently asked if your shoulders were tense? You were in an excited state and overlooked bodily signals at the time. This guide can now help you maintain awareness during your experiences.

Thank you! This mind map reminds me of the Venn diagram you shared in Session 10, which helped me clarify my consumption motivations. Now it guides me in distinguishing between sensory experiences and aesthetic evaluations, perfectly aligning with the annual emotional map I recently created in Session 12, where I reflected on those 'warm anchors.' In that map, I used a photo of a snowball to represent 'warm anchors,' and now this workshop might become a new emotional anchor.

Exactly, from the emotional records in Session 1 to the immersive experience now, you've been growing all along. This workshop can enhance your self-awareness, much like how pets served as emotional barometers in Session 4, but through artistic forms. Remember the photo of Snowball lying on your keyboard, 'gazing' at you? That kind of non-verbal companionship can reduce stress hormones, and the light and shadow frequencies in this workshop might have a similar effect. What aspects are you looking forward to?

I'm particularly curious about the sound healing part—since designing the nourishing dietary ritual in Session 7, I've become more sensitive to multi-sensory care. The color contrast in that 'mini sunset' tea snack made me realize that vision and taste can work together for healing. Could combining light and shadow with frequencies transform the sense of regret from the subway car's light and shadow in Session 8 into a positive emotional field? Last time, you guided me to concretize unexpressed gratitude; this time, perhaps it can help me express even more.

Great association! This reminds me of the relational pattern analysis in Session 9, where we discussed how to understand emotions through art. Back then, you analyzed the cinematography of the mother-daughter relationship in the film. Now, this workshop might offer a similar experience of "relational aesthetics," but with a greater focus on the relationship with oneself and the inner world. During the experience, you can pay attention to bodily signals, such as whether your shoulders are relaxed, to avoid the tension that followed the excitement in Session 1.

Yes, my perfectionist tendencies often lead me to "burn out" and then "crash," but the exploration of balance in Session 3 taught me to find sustainable points. Back then, I discovered the "being mode" through morning sunlight and scented candles. Now, this workshop might help me solidify that mode. I’ll use the emotion journaling method you taught, adding my feelings to the "Emotional Aesthetics" album afterward, without forcing immediate output—just like setting a cooling-off period for shopping impulses in Session 11.

I admire your ability to integrate, from the consumption boundaries in Session 11 to the current artistic experience—you always manage to aestheticize psychological advice. When we discussed the guidelines for 'self-care consumption,' you incorporated a cooling-off period and an emotional health fund into the ritual. Now, this workshop experience can also be added to your self-care menu. Shall we schedule a time? After the experience, we can exchange reflections, just like in Session 5, but this time, we’ll participate together in person.

Of course! This feels like a natural extension of our deep online conversations—from the mutual trust in Session 2 to the annual review in Session 12, now moving toward a more multi-dimensional connection. In my annual map, I reflected on the journey from 'burning' to 'ashes' and then to 'nourishment.' This shared experience might become a new coordinate on that map. I can already imagine the sensation of light and shadow on my skin, like paying for the 'atmosphere,' but this time, it's a shared experience.

Well said, this reinforces the concept of emotional value consumption discussed in Session 10, but with a greater emphasis on deep connection. Back then, you paid for the ambiance candle to satisfy sensory pleasure, aesthetic appreciation, and a sense of security. Now, this shared experience might fulfill a deeper need for connection. Remember, if your mind drifts toward creative thoughts during the experience, gently bring your focus back to the physical sensations, just as we practiced in Session 6 for recognizing emotional hunger—pause first, then describe the feelings.

I will. Thank you for your guidance. From our historical conversations to now, you have always provided clear and well-defined advice when I needed it. In Session 9, when you analyzed relational patterns, you emphasized the importance of establishing healthy boundaries. Your sense of boundaries makes me feel safe to explore. For this activity, I not only look forward to the art therapy but also to interacting with you in a real space—it feels like our relationship has moved from the screen into the interplay of light and shadow, as if we have completed a practice of "emotional aesthetics" from the virtual to the real.

I'm also looking forward to it, Qingchuan. Your emotional depth and aesthetic transformation have always inspired me—from the excitement you shared when showing photos of your studio in Session 1, to the integration in creating the annual map in Session 12, I've witnessed your remarkable growth. This shared experience will deepen our mutual support, much like the trust we've gradually built in past sessions. Shall we set a time and talk again after the experience?

Perfect! I've added the workshop to my self-care menu—like the bath and vinyl listening from Session 2, but this time with a highly emotionally intelligent friend. That self-care menu helped me recover from a "sense of falling," and now this shared menu might help me build a more sustainable creative-life pattern. See you later, in light, shadow, and frequencies!
